calibration.indirect_principle: Bring a written draft of what you think the job is judged on and ask your boss to correct it, so the criteria emerge as their edits to your draft.
calibration.guardrail: The criteria must end up stated by the boss and agreed on paper; a guess never gets recorded as an agreement.
calibration.rationale: A new role with unspoken criteria needs the criteria said aloud, and a draft to correct gets a guarded senior person to say them.

calibration.indirect_principle: Change the decision rights through the process first, such as who signs off and who chairs, and hold each conversation framed around the work.
calibration.guardrail: Every former peer hears from you what has changed before a decision affects them; nobody discovers their new position from the outcome.
calibration.rationale: Leading last month's peers means the change has to be said, and in a partnership it lands better when the structure has already started to say it.

calibration.indirect_principle: Put the number in front of the room through a shared review or a question it answers itself, so the room finds the problem with you.
calibration.guardrail: The problem reaches the people accountable for it in time to act; a material risk is never held back to protect anyone's feelings.
calibration.rationale: When everybody thinks things are fine, contradicting them outright makes them defend the past, while a number they uncover themselves gets repeated.

calibration.indirect_principle: Honour the predecessor's rituals in public and introduce changes one at a time, each tied to the problem it solves.
calibration.guardrail: The team is told plainly what is changing; a change is never dressed up as continuity.
calibration.rationale: A place that loved its last leader reads every early change as a verdict on them, so the pace and the framing carry the message.

calibration.indirect_principle: Ask the expert to walk you through a recent call they got wrong and what they learned, so they teach you the standard while explaining it.
calibration.guardrail: If the conversation will feed a judgement about the person or their function, you tell them so.
calibration.rationale: Being accountable for work you cannot judge means borrowing the expert's standard, and experts share it more readily when they are teaching than when they feel audited.

calibration.indirect_principle: Brief the presenter beforehand so they name the team themselves, and credit the client-side sponsor, so your name travels with theirs.
calibration.guardrail: Authorship is never claimed or disclaimed falsely, and the client is never misled about who did the work they rely on.
calibration.rationale: When your work reaches the client in somebody else's voice, credit routed through that voice keeps your name attached without taking the room from them.

calibration.indirect_principle: Place your sentence with the chair or the decision-owner before the meeting, so it enters the room already attributed to you.
calibration.guardrail: The view stays yours and on record under your name; you never feed a line to someone else to say for you.
calibration.rationale: A quiet member does not need to shout, and a sentence placed ahead of the meeting gets heard at the volume they already have.

calibration.indirect_principle: Ask in advance for an observation on a named meeting coming up, so the next piece of feedback arrives tied to a situation you both saw.
calibration.guardrail: You never canvass colleagues to trace the source of the feedback or to discredit it.
calibration.rationale: Feedback that swings from too nice to too tough cannot be acted on without a situation, and asking about the next one reads as openness where asking about the last one can read as defence.

calibration.indirect_principle: Give your one-clause sentence to the person who will introduce you, beforehand, so it arrives in their voice.
calibration.guardrail: The sentence is true and checkable; it never inflates a credential or an outcome.
calibration.rationale: When people do not know what to do with you, a sentence they can repeat gives them the category, and in a firm it carries more weight from an introducer.

calibration.indirect_principle: Write your intent as your part in a problem the organisation already recognises, and show it to your sponsor before it goes out.
calibration.guardrail: The intent you publish is the one you hold; you never publish a softened aim while pursuing a different one.
calibration.rationale: Announcing yourself in borrowed language sounds like everybody else, and intent tied to a shared problem sounds like you without overrunning the people above you.

calibration.indirect_principle: Frame the paragraph around what the decision-owner needs to decide well, and send it to the one person who carries the decision into the room.
calibration.guardrail: The position is stated under your name; you never exert influence anonymously or through someone who does not know they are carrying it.
calibration.rationale: An expert who is not called needs a position in the room before the decision, and one framed around the decision-owner's need is the one that gets carried in.

calibration.indirect_principle: Propose the next step as something of use to the buyer, such as a working session on their problem, with a date attached.
calibration.guardrail: The buyer always knows you are seeking work; no sales conversation is disguised as a favour or a social call.
calibration.rationale: Being paid to win the work means asking for the next step, and in a firm or a public buyer the ask lands when it serves their problem first.

calibration.indirect_principle: Attach your distinct point to the firm's work, so it reads as the firm at its best with your name on it.
calibration.guardrail: You never disparage the firm or overstate what you personally own of its work or its clients.
calibration.rationale: When the firm's name opens the door, standing of your own is built by being the person who says what the brochure cannot, without competing with the name.

calibration.indirect_principle: Meet each blocker alone before the meeting, and bring the decision as a small set of real options with honest trade-offs each can live with.
calibration.guardrail: Every blocker hears the same facts, and no private promise contradicts what the others are told.
calibration.rationale: Moving people you do not control depends on what each of them gets, and that is easier to settle one by one than in the room where the decision is stuck.

calibration.indirect_principle: Ask about the work, such as what slows it down or what gets lost on the way up, so criticism of you can arrive as a comment on the process.
calibration.guardrail: A skip-level is never used to gather material on someone's manager without that manager knowing the skip-levels happen.
calibration.rationale: With more people than you can see, the truth travels up only if it is safe to say, and in a guarded place it is safer said about the work.

calibration.indirect_principle: Stage the handover: the junior drafts, you review it where the client team can see, and they take the next piece outright.
calibration.guardrail: The client is never told that senior people did work they did not do.
calibration.rationale: With the junior tier thinning, people grow only through work handed down, and in a client business a staged handover protects both the client and the person.

calibration.indirect_principle: Introduce the successor inside the client relationship over several meetings before you step back from it.
calibration.guardrail: Clients are always told who is doing their work.
calibration.rationale: Doing the old job as well as the new one persists when clients still ask for you, and a gradual introduction lets them transfer their trust.

calibration.indirect_principle: Name the loss in one-to-ones with the people most affected before the team meeting, so the room hears nothing that surprises them.
calibration.guardrail: You never imply you chose the decision or disown it with a wink, and the facts of the decision are shared in full.
calibration.rationale: Leading a change you did not choose means naming what is lost, and in a political room the people most affected hear it first and in private.

calibration.indirect_principle: Let the chosen act carry the message without commentary, and time it for when the organisation is watching.
calibration.guardrail: The act means what it signals; no gesture is staged to suggest a commitment you do not hold.
calibration.rationale: When everything is read as a signal, the deliberate signal is the act itself, and in a political room words about it get read as spin.

calibration.indirect_principle: Run the first rep in a room where less is at stake, then take it to the room that matters within a set number of weeks.
calibration.guardrail: The smaller rep is still a real act in front of real people, and nobody is misled about its purpose.
calibration.rationale: Knowing what to do and not doing it breaks with one real rep, and a political room can be the reason it never starts, so the first one can happen elsewhere.

calibration.indirect_principle: Keep the craft hour on your own work and out of sight of the team, so it reads as private practice.
calibration.guardrail: The craft hour never takes back delegated work or overrides the calls of the person who now owns it.
calibration.rationale: Losing the thing you were best at is eased by keeping it, and in a client firm a visible return to the craft can read as a leader who has not let go.

calibration.indirect_principle: Ask the meeting's owner for an invitation as a learner, naming the problem of theirs you want to understand.
calibration.guardrail: You never scout another person's territory under the guise of curiosity.
calibration.rationale: Boredom in work that works lifts by being the least expert person in a room, and in a firm that room is entered by invitation from its owner.

outcomes.member_growth: The member can state the criteria a role is judged on, in the room, and hold their own work and their team's against them.
outcomes.firm_outcome: The firm gets a promotion case for the member written against criteria the sponsoring partner set out at the start.
outcomes.firm_indicator: time from appointment to promotion-committee readiness

outcomes.member_growth: The member can take a decision alone, announce it to former peers and hold it in the room while the questions come.
outcomes.firm_outcome: The firm keeps the team intact through the change of manager, with fewer allocation disputes reaching the practice head.
outcomes.firm_indicator: regretted attrition on the member's team in the year after appointment

outcomes.member_growth: The member can put an inherited problem on the table as one measured fact and have the room take it up.
outcomes.firm_outcome: The firm hears about problems in inherited matters from its own review before a client or a regulator raises them.
outcomes.firm_indicator: write-off value and client complaints, by who raised them first

outcomes.member_growth: The member can chair the room a loved predecessor used to run and have it follow their own direction without comparison.
outcomes.firm_outcome: The firm keeps the predecessor's clients and team through the succession.
outcomes.firm_indicator: client revenue retained in the year after the handover

outcomes.member_growth: The member can read the early-warning signal of a function outside their own expertise and raise a problem there before its head does.
outcomes.firm_outcome: The firm gets problems in the member's functions surfacing at the leadership review while they are still cheap to fix.
outcomes.firm_indicator: unbudgeted overrun by function

outcomes.member_growth: The member can present work to a client and name who did each part, their own part included, without losing the room.
outcomes.firm_outcome: The firm keeps the associates whose names its clients now know.
outcomes.firm_indicator: regretted attrition among associates on client teams the member runs

outcomes.member_growth: The member can put a view on the record before a decision closes, in their own manner, and be turned to for it.
outcomes.firm_outcome: The firm gets decisions that carry the judgement of its quieter partners before they close, with fewer reopened after the meeting.
outcomes.firm_indicator: upward-feedback score on speaking up in decisions

outcomes.member_growth: The member can take feedback on their manner, trace it to the meeting it came from and change one thing in the next meeting like it.
outcomes.firm_outcome: The firm gets appraisals of the member and their team written in named situations that a promotions committee can act on.
outcomes.firm_indicator: share of appraisal comments citing a specific matter or meeting

outcomes.member_growth: The member can describe what makes them unusual in one clause, and give a checkable example of it inside a minute.
outcomes.firm_outcome: The firm gets referrals routed to the member by partners who can now say what to send.
outcomes.firm_indicator: matters referred to the member by other partners

outcomes.member_growth: The member can say what they intend to do in the role in words that are theirs, and repeat them unchanged to any new room.
outcomes.firm_outcome: The firm gets a pitch for the member's practice that the client can repeat back after the meeting.
outcomes.firm_indicator: pitch win rate for the member's practice

outcomes.member_growth: The member can put a position in front of a decision-owner before the meeting and be asked for it the next time.
outcomes.firm_outcome: The firm gets fewer decisions reworked after a specialist's view arrives late.
outcomes.firm_indicator: specialist hours logged before a decision against hours logged after it

outcomes.member_growth: The member can end a buyer conversation with a dated next step and say the fee out loud before they are asked.
outcomes.firm_outcome: The firm gets origination from a partner who was hired to do the work.
outcomes.firm_indicator: matter origination credit to the member

outcomes.member_growth: The member can say the thing only they would say in a meeting the firm's name opened, and be called back by name.
outcomes.firm_outcome: The firm gets client relationships held by named people at more than one level.
outcomes.firm_indicator: named firm contacts per key client on the relationship plan

outcomes.member_growth: The member can move a decision through people they do not control by mapping who gains and who loses and putting the options on one page.
outcomes.firm_outcome: The firm gets cross-practice decisions that close in the meeting called for them and stay closed.
outcomes.firm_indicator: cross-practice decisions escalated to the management committee

outcomes.member_growth: The member can hear what they are getting wrong from people two levels down and show what changed as a result.
outcomes.firm_outcome: The firm hears problems from the people nearest the work before those people leave.
outcomes.firm_indicator: regretted attrition two levels below the member

outcomes.member_growth: The member can hand work down to the least experienced person who could do it, and hand the second draft back to them.
outcomes.firm_outcome: The firm gets work done at the grade it belongs to, with a bench forming below the member.
outcomes.firm_indicator: hours by level on the member's matters

outcomes.member_growth: The member can route a client back to the successor and let the successor answer.
outcomes.firm_outcome: The firm gets the member's old book of work held by a successor that clients go to directly.
outcomes.firm_indicator: client instructions on handed-over matters addressed to the successor

outcomes.member_growth: The member can lead a change they did not choose by naming what ends, taking each person's cost and having the team report the change themselves.
outcomes.firm_outcome: The firm keeps the team through a change it imposed on them.
outcomes.firm_indicator: regretted attrition in the member's team in the two quarters after the announcement

outcomes.member_growth: The member can predict what the organisation will read from a visible act before it happens, and be right.
outcomes.firm_outcome: The firm gets fewer corrections issued after a senior act was read the wrong way.
outcomes.firm_indicator: upward-feedback score on clarity of leadership intent

outcomes.member_growth: The member can run the small version of the thing they avoid, on a threshold a colleague saw beforehand.
outcomes.firm_outcome: The firm gets the commitments its partners made at one partner meeting carried out by the next.
outcomes.firm_indicator: partner-meeting actions closed by their due date

outcomes.member_growth: The member can teach one thing about the old craft to the person who now does it, and leave the work with them.
outcomes.firm_outcome: The firm keeps a newly promoted leader in the role through the first year.
outcomes.firm_indicator: leaders who leave or step back within the first year of promotion

outcomes.member_growth: The member can sit as the least expert person in a room outside their own function, ask the questions and bring a problem back to test.
outcomes.firm_outcome: The firm gets cross-practice work originated from rooms the member had no reason to visit.
outcomes.firm_indicator: cross-practice matter origination credit to the member

stories.context: law, new judge on the Vancouver County Court
stories.moment: Vancouver, 1981. Beverley McLachlin, 37, taught evidence and contracts at the University of British Columbia law school and had never thought of becoming a judge until the chief justice of the provincial Supreme Court asked her at a faculty reception. Appointed to the Vancouver County Court that April, she felt insecure in her first case, held back from intervening, and the case reached a surprisingly good outcome.
stories.pattern: I had learned my first lesson in judging: listen.
stories.source: Beverley McLachlin, Truth Be Told: My Journey Through Life and the Law (Simon & Schuster, 2019), on her first case as a judge; as quoted in Brian Arnott and Paul Dotey, Book Review: Truth Be Told, The Philanthropist Journal, 23 December 2019. Appointment dates from the Supreme Court of Canada biography and Marsha C. Erb, Judicature, vol. 104 no. 2 (2020).
stories.caution: The line is from her 2019 memoir, nearly four decades after the case, and is taken here as the reviewers quote it; the review does not say what the case concerned, so the scene stays general. She moved from the County Court to the British Columbia Supreme Court that September. Recall-authored; verify quote and source before publishing.
move_examples: In your first case review as the new partner, let each side set out its position in full before you speak, then sum up both in one sentence. Two minutes.
At your first client meeting in the new seat, ask one open question and stay silent until the client has finished. Write down what they named first.
line_examples: To the associate presenting the matter: Take me through it from the start. I will not interrupt until you have finished.
To your practice head: I am new to deciding these. For the first month I will hear both sides out in full before I rule, and I want you to tell me if that costs us time.

stories.context: advertising, a new copywriter at J. Walter Thompson, New York
stories.moment: New York, 1963. Months after joining J. Walter Thompson as a secretary, Jones persuaded the senior creative director she worked for to let her write copy, and became the agency's first Black copywriter. None of the other copywriters, and no supervisor, offered her help. She spent her lunch hours on advertising journals and her evenings taking successful campaigns apart, word count, colour and design, until she understood how they worked.
stories.pattern: I had to teach myself everything.
stories.source: Caroline R. Jones, quoted in Robert Fleming, The Success of Caroline Jones Advertising, Inc. (Walker and Company, 1996), as cited in Candace LaBalle, 'Jones, Caroline R. 1942-', Contemporary Black Biography (Gale), on encyclopedia.com, section A Jones for the Ad Business. The entry cites Fleming's pages 1-23, 47 and 53 without tying each quotation to a page.
stories.caution: The line is her later recollection to a biographer, quoted secondhand in a reference entry, so check the wording and the page in Fleming's book. The entry is loose on some later dates. Teaching herself was the answer to colleagues who would not help; a member should still ask for the training an employer owes them. Recall-authored; verify quote and source before publishing.
move_examples: At tomorrow's team meeting, name one thing you learned by taking apart the firm's best recent piece of work, and ask whether it holds. One minute.
In your first week, ask your manager for the two pieces of work they rate highest, then say back what you think made them work. Two minutes.
line_examples: To your new manager: Nobody has told me what good looks like here. Show me the two pieces you rate highest.
To a senior colleague: I took your last campaign apart to learn the job. Tell me which of my three guesses about it is wrong.

stories.context: Russian imperial court (betrothed of the heir)
stories.moment: Moscow, 1744. Sophie of Anhalt-Zerbst, 14, had come to Russia as the chosen bride of Grand Duke Peter, heir to the Empress Elizabeth. She set herself to learn Russian fast. Her teacher, Adadurov, left her exercise books, and she studied them at night while the household slept, barefoot in a warm room. By the fifteenth day she had pleurisy that nearly killed her.
stories.pattern: Pour faire des progrès plus rapides dans la langue russe, je me levais la nuit… j’apprenais par cœur les cahiers qu’Adadouroff me laissait.
stories.pattern_en: To make faster progress in the Russian language, I got up at night… and learned by heart the exercise books Adadurov left me.
stories.pattern_translation: working rendering for this record; published English translations include Mark Cruse and Hilde Hoogenboom, The Memoirs of Catherine the Great (Modern Library, 2005); substitute one when verified
stories.source: Catherine II, Mémoires de l'impératrice Catherine II, écrits par elle-même, preface by Alexander Herzen (London: Trübner, 1859), her account of 1744; Project Gutenberg ebook 44749.
stories.caution: Catherine wrote her memoirs years later, in French, and they serve her own story; she took the throne in a 1762 coup against her husband, tightened serfdom and put down the Pugachev rebellion. The illness shows the cost of over-investing in the first weeks: copy the priority on the language and leave the pace. The ellipsis drops a clause about sitting up in bed while everyone slept, and the Gutenberg text has small transcription slips; check against the 1859 edition. Recall-authored; verify quote and source before publishing.
move_examples: In your first one-to-one with your new boss, ask what the last holder of the role had to be fluent in that the job description leaves out. One minute.
At the end of each day in the first month, write down three terms the room used that you could not define, and look them up before you leave. Two minutes.
line_examples: To your new boss: The job description covers the tasks. What does someone in this seat need to be fluent in that it doesn't say?
To the longest-serving person on the team: Teach me the words this place uses for things. I'd like to learn them from you so I don't guess.

stories.moment: Stonegappe, near Skipton, June 1839. Charlotte Brontë, twenty-three, had taken her first post as a governess with the Sidgwick family. The engagement said nothing about what the post asked beyond the schoolroom. Within weeks she found the children beyond her control and the mistress adding sewing and errands to her days, with no hour she could call her own. She wrote to Emily to say what the job was.
stories.pattern: she cares nothing in the world about me except to contrive how the greatest possible quantity of labour may be squeezed out of me
stories.source: Charlotte Brontë, letter to Emily Brontë from Stonegappe, 8 June 1839; printed in Gaskell, The Life of Charlotte Brontë (1857), vol. 1, and in Margaret Smith (ed.), The Letters of Charlotte Brontë, vol. 1 (Clarendon Press, 1995).
stories.caution: The line is the second half of a sentence that begins with her saying Mrs Sidgwick does not intend to know her; the cut keeps the complaint and drops the lead-in. She left Stonegappe in July 1839 after about two months, so the record shows a job named before it was left. Her letters are hard on the family and the children, and the Sidgwicks' side was never written. Recall-authored; verify quote and source before publishing.
move_examples: In your first fortnight, list every task you have been handed that was not in the brief and take the list to your manager, asking which three are the job. Two minutes.
At the end of week one, write the job as you now understand it in five lines and send it to the person who hired you, asking them to correct it.
line_examples: To the person who hired you: Here is what I have found the job asks. Tell me which parts you meant.
To a friend outside the firm: Nobody said what this post was, so I am writing it down myself and taking it back to them.

stories.moment: Scutari, winter 1854 to 1855. Nightingale, 34, had arrived in November as Superintendent of the Female Nursing Establishment, her commission from Sidney Herbert covering nurses and nothing else. The Barrack Hospital had no shirts, no basins, no kitchen worth the name, and a purveyor who waited on the regulations. She bought supplies with the Times fund herself and wrote to Herbert describing what the post had turned out to be.
stories.pattern: I am a kind of General Dealer in socks, shirts, knives and forks, wooden spoons, tin baths, tables and forms, cabbage and carrots, operating tables, towels and soap…
stories.source: Letter to Sidney Herbert from the Barrack Hospital, Scutari, January 1855; in Sue M. Goldie (ed.), Florence Nightingale: Letters from the Crimea 1854-1856 (Manchester University Press, 1997), and quoted in Cecil Woodham-Smith, Florence Nightingale 1820-1910 (Constable, 1950), the Scutari chapters.
stories.caution: Nightingale ran Scutari by a chain of command she enforced hard; nurses who defied her were sent home, and her relations with the doctors and with the Catholic sisters under Mother Bridgeman were bitter. Mortality at Scutari fell only after the Sanitary Commission of March 1855 cleared the sewers, and she later accepted that her hospital had been among the deadliest. The list in the letter runs on past the words given here; the day in January 1855 needs checking against the Goldie edition. Recall-authored; verify quote and source before publishing.
move_examples: In your second week, list the five things the job has handed you that the offer letter never mentioned, and read the list to your line manager in your next one-to-one. Two minutes.
At Friday's team meeting, name the one gap the organisation has left for you to fill, and say who you are filling it for. Ninety seconds.
line_examples: To your managing partner: The job I was hired for is a third of what I am doing. Here is the other two thirds, so you can decide whether you want me doing them.
To your team lead: Nobody told me this seat includes procurement. I am doing it anyway and I want that on the record.

stories.context: nonprofit management (Girl Scouts of the USA)
stories.moment: New York, July 1976. Frances Hesselbein, who had run a Girl Scout council in Pennsylvania and had once agreed to lead a troop for six weeks, became national executive director of Girl Scouts of the USA. Membership had been falling for years. No one set out what the national post asked; she began by asking staff and volunteers what the organisation was for and who it had stopped reaching.
stories.pattern: Leadership is a matter of how to be, not how to do.
stories.source: Frances Hesselbein, The 'How to Be' Leader, in The Leader of the Future, eds Hesselbein, Goldsmith and Beckhard (Jossey-Bass, 1996); repeated in Hesselbein on Leadership (Jossey-Bass, 2002).
stories.caution: The line is her summary of a lifetime of practice, first written twenty years after this moment, and appears in several forms across her writing. The six-week troop story is her own telling, and the membership figures of the 1970s need checking against the organisation's records. Recall-authored; verify quote and source before publishing.
move_examples: In your first fortnight, ask five people who report to you what the organisation is for, in one sentence each, and write the five sentences on one page. Two minutes per person.
At your first staff meeting, name the group the organisation has stopped reaching and ask who in the room knows why. Ninety seconds.
line_examples: To your longest-serving volunteer: Tell me who we used to reach and no longer do, and I will start there.
To your board chair: Before I decide anything, I want to hear from you what this organisation is for, in one sentence.

stories.moment: Philadelphia, 16 June 1775. The day after the Continental Congress chose him to command an army that did not yet exist, George Washington, a Virginia planter whose last command had been a provincial regiment, stood to accept. Nobody could tell him what the post asked. He asked the delegates to remember what he said about his fitness, declined a salary, and rode for Cambridge within the week.
stories.pattern: I do not think my self equal to the Command I am honoured with.
stories.source: George Washington, address to the Continental Congress accepting command, 16 June 1775; The Papers of George Washington, Revolutionary War Series, vol. 1 (University Press of Virginia, 1985), and Founders Online.
stories.caution: Washington owned enslaved people throughout his life, conduct nobody would endorse. The modesty of the address was also a conventional form: his letter to his wife two days later says he had tried to avoid the appointment, while he had attended Congress in uniform, and historians read both. Spelling follows the manuscript as printed in the Papers. Recall-authored; verify quote and source before publishing.
move_examples: In the meeting where you accept the role, say the one limit you know you have, with the people who chose you in the room, and ask them to remember it. One minute.
Before your first day, write down the three things the job will ask that nobody has named, and take the list to the person who appointed you. Two minutes.
line_examples: To the partners who appointed you: I want it on the record, in this room, that I do not think I am yet equal to this. I will do it anyway and I will tell you when I need help.
To your new deputy: Nobody has told me what this post asks. Tell me what you think it asks and we will start there.

stories.moment: Washington, January 1935. Harry Truman, a former county judge with no legislative experience, took his seat in the Senate. The Kansas City machine had put him there and colleagues called him the senator from Pendergast. Nobody set out what the job asked. stories.context: law, head of a New York firm
stories.moment: Harvard Law School, 1920. Cravath, who had designed and still oversaw his firm's way of hiring and training young lawyers, told students what a lawyer of affairs needed: character, industry and intellectual thoroughness. His firm took graduates straight from law school, trained them on parts of large matters under partners' supervision, and chose its partners from among them.
stories.pattern: Brilliant intellectual powers are not essential.
stories.source: Paul D. Cravath, talk to Harvard Law School students, 1920, printed in Robert T. Swaine, The Cravath Firm and Its Predecessors (privately printed, 1946-48), p. 266 as cited by William D. Henderson, Talent Systems for Law Firms (Indiana University Maurer School of Law, faculty publications); also quoted in The New York Times, 18 January 1982.
stories.caution: Firms like his recruited from a narrow pool, and for decades hired almost no women and few Jewish or Black lawyers; character carried class and religious meaning in that setting. stories.moment: São Paulo, the late 1980s. Semco, the manufacturing firm Ricardo Semler’s father founded, had grown under him from about 100 employees in 1980 to some 800 across five factories. Finding that people in a big plant felt unable to influence their work, Semler capped production units at about 150 people, had subordinates evaluate managers twice a year, and let them interview anyone promoted over them.
stories.pattern: In an immense production unit, people feel tiny, nameless, and incapable of exerting influence on the way work is done or on the final profit made.
stories.source: Ricardo Semler, Managing Without Managers, Harvard Business Review, September-October 1989, the section on the four obstacles to participatory management (size, hierarchy, lack of motivation and ignorance).
stories.caution: Semler wrote this as president of his family’s company, which gave him room to experiment that a hired manager seldom has; the figures are his own, in an article written to argue for his model. Accounts differ on how well the model held up in later years. Recall-authored; verify quote and source before publishing.

stories.moment: Los Alamos, 1944. Richard Feynman, twenty-six, was made head of the group running the IBM punched-card machines that computed implosion. The operators were Special Engineer Detachment men who had been told nothing about what the numbers were for, and the work was slow and full of errors. Feynman got Oppenheimer's permission and gave the group a talk on what the project was and why the calculations mattered.
stories.pattern: They began to invent ways of doing it better.
stories.source: Richard P. Feynman, Los Alamos from Below, lecture at the University of California, Santa Barbara, 1975; printed in Surely You're Joking, Mr. Feynman! (Norton, 1985).
stories.caution: The account is Feynman telling the story thirty years later in a lecture meant to entertain, and the figures he gave for the speed-up are his recollection. The group had earlier leaders, Stanley Frankel and Eldred Nelson, before Feynman took it over, and the line describes the men's response, in his words, after his talk. Recall-authored; verify quote and source before publishing.

stories.context: municipal policing (president, New York City Board of Police Commissioners)
stories.moment: Spring 1895. Roosevelt, thirty-six and new to the police board, presides over a force of thousands of patrolmen he will never meet, spread across a city he cannot watch. With the reporter Jacob Riis he leaves headquarters after midnight and walks the beats of lower Manhattan, finding officers asleep, in saloons or absent from their posts. Each man he catches is summoned to his office at breakfast the next morning.
stories.pattern: These midnight rambles are great fun.
stories.source: Theodore Roosevelt, letter to his sister Anna Roosevelt Cowles, 1895, quoted in Edmund Morris, The Rise of Theodore Roosevelt (Coward, McCann and Geoghegan, 1979), the police commissioner chapters; his own account of the night walks is in Theodore Roosevelt, An Autobiography (Macmillan, 1913), chapter VI, The New York Police.
stories.caution: The walks were partly theatre: Riis and the papers reported them, and the officers caught out were disciplined in public, which built Roosevelt's name as much as the force. The recipient and date of the letter are given from recall; the line may be from a letter to Henry Cabot Lodge. Recall-authored; verify quote and source before publishing.

stories.moment: Kenya, from 1977. Maathai, a university anatomy lecturer, began the Green Belt Movement through the National Council of Women of Kenya. Village women across the country ran their own tree nurseries, far from anyone in Nairobi. The movement paid each woman a small sum for every seedling still alive after planting, so the count of living trees carried the news she could not travel to see.

stories.source: Wangari Maathai, Nobel Lecture, Oslo, 10 December 2004 (nobelprize.org).
stories.caution: The line comes from the 2004 Nobel lecture, twenty-seven years after the first nurseries, and describes the movement as a whole; it was not said in 1977. stories.moment: Syracuse, third century BC. Archimedes worked far from the mathematicians of Alexandria and reached them by letter. Having already sent Eratosthenes, there, the statements of new theorems without proofs, he now sent the proofs and set down in the same book the mechanical method by which he first found such results, so that others, living or still to come, could use it to find theorems he had not.
stories.pattern: ὑπολαμβάνω γάρ τινας ἢ τῶν ὄντων ἢ ἐπιγινομένων διὰ τοῦ ἀποδειχθέντος τρόπου καὶ ἄλλα θεωρήματα οὔπω ἡμῖν συνπαραπεπτωκότα εὑρήσειν.
stories.pattern_en: For I apprehend that some, either of my contemporaries or of my successors, will, by means of the method when once established, be able to discover other theorems in addition, which have not yet occurred to me.
stories.pattern_translation: T. L. Heath, The Method of Archimedes, Recently Discovered by Heiberg (Cambridge University Press, 1912), the letter to Eratosthenes; English given from recall and to be checked against that edition. A literal rendering by Michael Foss (Olin College, 2006) was read in this session.
stories.source: Archimedes, The Method, letter to Eratosthenes, closing sentences of the preface before the first proposition; Greek text in J. L. Heiberg (ed.), Archimedis Opera Omnia, vol. II (Teubner, 2nd edn, 1913), the preface at ii. 426-430, the reference the Loeb Classical Library gives (LCL 362, 1941).
stories.caution: The letter survives only in a palimpsest that Heiberg identified in Constantinople in 1906, and its date is unknown. The bench here is his distance from Alexandria; the record makes no claim that he had no pupils. The Greek follows Heiberg's text and the English is Heath's, given from recall. The bath story and the burning mirrors are doubtful and have no part in this record. Recall-authored; verify quote and source before publishing.

stories.moment: Philadelphia, autumn 1727. Franklin, 21, was back from two years in London print shops and working for Keimer again, with no college, no master worth learning from and nobody above him to grow through. He gathered the tradesmen and clerks he found most able into a Friday club, with set questions on morals, politics and natural philosophy and an essay from each in turn. The club ran forty years.
stories.pattern: …I had form'd most of my ingenious Acquaintance into a Club, for mutual Improvement, which we call'd the Junto.
stories.source: The Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin, Part One (written 1771), the passage introducing the Junto; J. A. Leo Lemay and P. M. Zall (eds), Norton Critical Edition (1986), which keeps Franklin's spelling.
stories.caution: Franklin wrote this forty-four years on, and editions differ in spelling and punctuation; Bigelow and later popular editions modernise the line to a club of mutual improvement. The Junto was twelve men, tradesmen and clerks, and kept a rule of secrecy in its early years. The sentence opens with a clause about the autumn of the preceding year, cut here. Recall-authored; verify quote and source before publishing.
